new_statements.quote: The vowels of Chuj are high and low front vowels i and e, low central a and low and high back rounded vowels o and u. Strong stress in words is generally on the vowel of the root, with secondary stress on final syllables. While marking stress is not part of the official orthography and is not necessary for native speakers, in other works—and in the text analysis below—I have added accent marks on the strong syllables to help the nonnative reader appreciate the rhythm of speech.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) stress falls on the vowel of the lexical root, wherever the root sits in the inflected word (Chuj roots are mostly CVC monosyllables, so root stress is often word-initial or after prefixes); word-final syllables carry a secondary stress. Hopkins's stress-marked text analysis (e.g. 7áy wal jun yík'ti7 ko mám kícham chí7 7áy kaníh, p. 136ff.) shows the root vowel accented in each word. Consistent with this, Hopkins 2012 (dictionary intro, p. xi) marks [stúk.wi.ch'al.wính], root of the verb stressed, incorporated object noun ch'al unstressed. The ALMG descriptive grammar (García Pablo & Domingo Pascual 2007, sec. 1.12, pp. 67-68) instead opens with the pan-Mayan claim that stress is 'agudo', always on the final syllable, then lists Chuj examples with penultimate stress on disyllabic roots (Kób'es, Cháb'in, Tzímin, Chítam, Chíb'ej) and others with final stress (Mách, Hachtík, T'akwalíl, Pixán, Unín); the normative grammar (Domingo Pascual 2007, p. 81) says stress is non-contrastive and 'la mayoría de las palabras tienen acento agudo'. So the native-academy grammars lean final, the linguist's description is root-based with final secondary stress; the two agree on monosyllabic-root words (which are the majority).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Hopkins 2021 p. 127: secondary stress on final syllables. Bennett 2016 (sec. 6.1.1, p. 496) lists Hopkins 1967 among impressionistic secondary-stress reports for Mayan to be treated with caution.
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' (Hopkins 2021). Incorporated object nouns in noun-incorporation compounds are obligatorily unstressed (Hopkins 2021 p. 134; Hopkins 2012 p. xi); directional-motion particles come in unstressed (+5) and stressed (+6) series; noun classifiers vary in stress and are unstressed before a noun (Hopkins 2021 pp. 130-135). ALMG 2007 descriptive grammar: loans sometimes keep Spanish stress (Kalnél ~ kalnelú, Animá, B'urú, Keneyá).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('stress in words'), with the final-syllable secondary stress phrased at word level; Hopkins's marked texts are running narrative, and Hopkins 2012's example [stúk.wi.ch'al.wính] shows a phrase-final classifier winh bearing stress, so phrase-final prominence is also in play. Stress is not written in the ALMG orthography and is non-contrastive (Domingo Pascual 2007 p. 81).
new_statements.identity_note: chuj1251 is a Glottolog "Bookkeeping" code with zero descriptive references of its own: it stands for the retired ISO 639-3 code [cnm] "Chuj, Ixtatán", merged into [cac] Chuj by ISO change request 2008-050. Every source examined describes Chuj proper, Glottolog chuj1250 (mostly the San Mateo Ixtatán variety; Hopkins's data are San Mateo Ixtatán 1964-65). chuj1250 already has an check folder with the same Hopkins 2021 file; the catalog entry should be filed under chuj1250, with chuj1251 treated as an alias, not a second language (a retired code does not make a separate language).
